headline: Diamondback Bite Behind San Antonio Hooters Leads to Firing Allegations in Federal Court
summary: A dishwasher alleges a diamondback rattlesnake bit his finger while cleaning behind a San Antonio Hooters, and that he was later fired while recovering. He is now suing HMC Hospitality Group for FMLA violations and workers' compensation retaliation.
body:
It starts with a snake and ends in federal court. I'm Philip Massouh, and this is SnakeNews. We're coming to you tonight with a story out of San Antonio, Texas, where a man says a diamondback rattlesnake bit his left middle finger while he was cleaning the lot behind a Hooters restaurant. His name is Alejandro Aleman, and he says he was later fired while he was still recovering, with no reason given. The court fight is about the return, not the snake. Let's get into it.

Rattlesnakes are ordinary wildlife in this city. In August 2025, local news reported that bites rise in peak summer months, when people are outdoors more, and named copperheads, cottonmouths and rattlesnakes among the most common snakes here. But this bite happened in October, behind a restaurant. Aleman called emergency medical personnel and was taken to University Hospital that day. He received a letter excusing him from work through October 13. He was discharged on October 7 with prescriptions for pain and infection and referrals to the hospital's trauma clinic. He experienced tingling and numbness in his hand.

The lawsuit says Aleman kept his manager informed by text. The manager told him, "don't worry about anything, we've got it covered." After an October 14 appointment, his return still depended on a doctor's approval. A medical provider completed a Texas workers' compensation work-status report after that visit. He was restricted from returning through October 28, and use of his left hand was restricted through November 11. A work-status report stated "no dishwasher work."

He missed about eight weeks on medical leave and received workers' compensation benefits during that time off. A November 18 follow-up released him to return on November 28, a day he was also scheduled to work. He returned on December 1.

But when he showed up, he could not clock in. His manager told him to work the shift anyway and said the login would be fixed when the general manager returned from vacation. Aleman worked the entire week after coming back, and he alleges he was not paid for the shifts he worked after returning.

The general manager returned on December 8 and asked, "what are you doing working here today?" The complaint alleges HMC terminated Aleman before the general manager saw him working, and that no reason was given. He alleges the discharge was for reporting the injury, seeking treatment, taking qualifying Family and Medical Leave Act leave, and receiving workers' compensation benefits.

Aleman has sued HMC Hospitality Group Inc., a Clearwater, Florida company, in San Antonio federal court, accusing it of violating the Family and Medical Leave Act and retaliating against him for filing a workers' compensation claim. He is seeking unspecified damages. The lawsuit was filed by attorney Michael V. Galo Jr. Neither Galo nor an HMC spokeswoman immediately responded to a request for comment, according to the San Antonio Express-News.

Under federal leave rules, individuals, not only employees, are protected from retaliation for opposing a practice unlawful under the Act. That general rule does not establish whether Aleman or HMC met the Act's coverage tests, and it does not decide this case. The docket lists Aleman v. HMC Hospitality Group, Inc., No. 5:2026cv07187, as a Family and Medical Leave Act case filed November 13 in the Western District of Texas.

The restaurant opened in 2017. The complaint says HMC took it over from TW Restaurant Holder LLC in October 2025, the month of the bite, and was that company's successor in interest. TW Restaurant Holder LLC filed for bankruptcy protection with Hooters of America LLC in Dallas in 2025. On October 31, 2025, Hooters Original Founders' Group, led by CEO Neil Kiefer, acquired Hooters of America with Hoot Owl Restaurants LLC as a partner. The group said it would own and operate about 140 of the chain's 198 U.S. restaurants, and it planned menu, uniform and restaurant upgrades. Aleman's suit is against HMC.

Now, the SnakeNews Safety Desk. I want you to listen closely, because this is important. If a diamondback rattlesnake ever bites you or someone near you, call 911 right away. Stay as calm and still as you can. Keep the bitten limb still, and ideally at or below the level of your heart. Remove any tight clothing or jewelry near the bite before swelling starts. Do not use a tourniquet. Do not cut the wound. Do not try to suck out the venom. Those old tricks can make things worse. The snake in this story is a diamondback rattlesnake, a venomous pit viper, and rattlesnakes are ordinary wildlife in San Antonio. So if you are in snake country, watch your hands and feet, especially around tall grass, brush, or behind buildings where a snake might be hiding.

Here at SnakeNews, we don't take sides in a legal fight, but we do take snake safety seriously. A diamondback rattlesnake is not a creature to ignore, and a bite can change a life in an instant. That's why we bring you the Safety Desk every single night.

And now, the Santa Monica check-in. I'm Philip Massouh, and I'm fine. No snakes under the anchor desk tonight, no rattles in the studio. But I'm watching the shadows, because if a snake can show up behind a Hooters in San Antonio, it can show up anywhere. Stay safe, stay alert, and keep your fingers away from dark corners.

For SnakeNews, I'm Philip Massouh. Good night.
